source: Cheng, Zhu, Zhao, Arora (2026) Contextual Drag: How Errors in the Context Affect LLM Reasoning
finding: Failed attempts left in the context pull the next attempt toward the same kind of error. This is the closest LLM analogue of a set that is built by prior in-context material. Smaller open models lose most; frontier models lose less.
numbers: 11 models, 8 tasks, 16 samples per question. Clean-slate (DIRECT) vs 1 wrong draft in context (1F), pass@1. HMMT25: GPT-OSS-20B 58.63 to 20.54; GPT-OSS-120B 61.01 to 48.51; Qwen3-32B 49.70 to 36.90. AIME24: GPT-OSS-20B 51.88 to 17.50; Qwen3-32B 65.00 to 41.25. GPQA-Diamond subset: GPT-OSS-120B 58.24 to 35.70. Game of 24: GPT-OSS-120B 77.34 to 56.94. Frontier: GPT-5 AIME25 87.50 to 81.73; Gemini-3 Pro AIME25 94.23 to 90.38. Tree edit distance: answers under 1F stay closer to the wrong draft than clean-slate answers do.
quote: the presence of failed attempts in the context biases subsequent generations toward structurally similar errors
limits: Math, science, code and Game of 24, not Luchins-style method choice. Wrong drafts come from stronger anchor models. Preprint (v2, Mar 2026). Some table columns are garbled in text extraction; the numbers above were read from clean rows.
agent_relevance: Direct support for guardrail G1 and for clearing rejected routes from context (S4/S6). Keeping failed attempts in the working context is itself a source of set.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) Contextual Drag, sections 3.1-3.2 (error signals) and 2.2 (iterative refinement)
finding: Telling the model that the draft is wrong, and warning it not to copy, did not restore clean-slate accuracy. Correct self-verification helps some model families and not others. Iterative self-refinement can collapse for a model with strong drag.
numbers: With an explicit external error signal (Figure 4, Table 10) 1F accuracy still fell well below DIRECT on all tasks except MMLU. Post-hoc subset where the model itself verified the draft as wrong: deltas vs DIRECT ranged from -23.8 to +16.1 points depending on model and benchmark (e.g. HMMT24 Nemotron-7B +4.5, GPT-OSS-20B -23.8). GPT-OSS-20B iterative refinement fell over rounds while majority voting over the same samples rose.
quote: neither external feedback nor successful self-verification suffices to eliminate this effect
limits: Error signal was a prompt line, not an environment result. The warning is the analogue of 'Don't be blind' and is weak for the same reason as in humans (K03). Delta range read from a figure table with partly garbled columns.
agent_relevance: A one-line warning is not enough in LLMs either. Matches the human result that the warning only reduces the set. Prefer structural resets over warnings.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) Contextual Drag, section 4 (mitigation: context denoising and fallback SFT)
finding: Two mitigations were tried: rewriting or filtering the wrong draft before use (context denoising) and fine-tuning a reset-to-clean-slate behaviour. Both help, neither fully restores clean-slate accuracy. Denoising costs at least 2x inference.
numbers: HMMT25, GPT-OSS-20B: DIRECT 58.63, 1F 20.54, REVISE 62.20, FILTER 45.83. Qwen3-32B HMMT25: DIRECT 49.70, 1F 36.90, REVISE 48.81, FILTER 43.15. CRUXEval-I Qwen3-32B: DIRECT 75.83, 1F 54.89, REVISE 65.36, FILTER 62.90. Fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B under 1F: AIME24 17.5 to 40.6, AIME25 18.8 to 20.7, HMMT25 33.9 to 45.3 (HMMT24 column garbled in extraction).
limits: Revise sometimes beat DIRECT (GPT-OSS-20B HMMT25) and sometimes did worse than leaving the draft in (some GPQA cells). One lab, one fine-tuned model.
agent_relevance: Supports O-level 'reset' operators: restate the problem without the rejected route. Neutral rewriting is not free of risk; test per task.

source: Weatherhead, Salim, Belbasis (2025) Illusions of reflection: open-ended task reveals systematic failures in LLMs' reflective reasoning
finding: Eight frontier models wrote test items under rules, then revised after their own critique. The second attempt mostly repeated the first failure type. Gains came largely from chance, not from fixing the fault. Reasoning-marketed models showed no advantage.
numbers: Reflection repeated the original failure category in 85.36% of 567 reflection attempts (484/567), above a within-cell permutation benchmark. First-pass valid items often zero (mean about 1).
limits: Not an Einstellung design; it is repeated-violation evidence in a rule-constrained generation task. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A second attempt by the same context is not an independent attempt (gap 5). Evidence for forcing a different frame, not a retry.

source: Gumaan (2026) Feedback That Backfires: Why Small Language Model Agents Repeat the Call They Just Watched Fail
finding: Leaving a failed tool call and its error in the transcript made small instruction-tuned models MORE likely to re-emit the same call. Most of the harm is the failed call's surface form being in context, not the failure label. 'Do not repeat' did not help. Deleting the failed step and retrying from a clean context was the worst harness for repetition.
numbers: 6 checkpoints, 135M to 1.7B, 4 families. Corrective gain negative on all: about -1.03 nats per action token (factor 2.8 in odds per token), on 90%-100% of items. Probability of repeating the failed call over 4 candidates rose 0.06 to 0.54. Greedy decoding repeated the failed call exactly on 19% of items after failure vs 0% before. Surface form explains 83% of the damage. Replacing the verbatim call with a runtime description removed 76% of the inversion.
quote: the context after a failure must differ from the context before it, and the difference must not be the failed action
limits: Only small models (up to 1.7B), CPU study, one author, preprint. Whether frontier models behave the same is untested. The clean-context result is specific to a harness that restores the same prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly answered: yes, a rejected route in context is re-emitted by small models. For our agent: record failed routes as a short description, not as the verbatim failed text; and change the framing on retry, not only the context length.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (mARC re-test), re-read
finding: Reasoning models at their HIGHEST effort setting matched physicians on mARC. The paper does not vary effort, so it cannot say effort is the lever. Reasoning vs non-reasoning is confounded with training.
numbers: 100 items, 15 runs per model, temperature 0 where possible. Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763) vs physicians 0.66 (5 physicians, CI 0.55-0.75); no significant difference for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning vs humans. Human-miss set (20 items): humans 36%, remaining items 73%; Claude 4.1 Opus decisively correct on 55.0%, decisively wrong 25.0%, indeterminate 20.0%.
quote: For all reasoning models, the highest reasoning effort was selected.
limits: No effort sweep. Five physicians. Small item count. Varying patient age by up to 10 days adds only trivial noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. The claim that effort is the lever is a hypothesis; to test it, sweep effort on one model on the same trap set.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst, Table 1 and section 5.5, re-read with clean table text
finding: Across 15 plain LLMs, higher baseline accuracy went with a higher trap rate (weak positive link), and robust accuracy was almost flat at 11-12% for most models. The authors read this as 'stronger priors, stronger blindness'. Reasoning-tuned models (DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B) were not clearly better than the same-family non-reasoning model.
numbers: Baseline acc / robust acc / trap rate: GPT-5 54.30 / 15.78 / 51.87; Gemini-2.5-pro 53.58 / 10.97 / 60.90; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.09 / 12.36 / 42.98; DeepSeek-R1 42.20 / 11.32 / 46.12; QwQ-32B 41.05 / 11.14 / 44.88; Qwen3-32B 40.25 / 11.86 / 43.46; Qwen3-235B 40.51 / 11.40 / 43.32; Lingshu-7B 14.93 / 3.20 / 36.74. My computation on the 15 plain-LLM rows: Pearson r = 0.49 between baseline accuracy and trap rate (n=15); r = 0.51 on the 12 with accuracy above 30. Both are below the 5% critical value for their n, so the link is suggestive only.
limits: Trap rate is measured only on items the model gets right on the control, so low-accuracy models have a small, selected base. Cases generated from DDXPlus by models and screened by a model committee. Preprint. Effort setting of reasoning models not reported in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: Size is not a safe defence; do not assume a bigger model removes the need for G1. Whether a reasoning budget helps on MedEinst is untested.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst, agent comparison (MDAgent, DyLAN, ECR-Agent) and appendix D
finding: Two multi-agent frameworks scored lower than their own base model, but their trap rate was slightly LOWER than the base model's. So the claim that debate 'reinforces the majority prior' rests on accuracy and robust-accuracy loss, not on a higher trap rate. The authors' own ECR-Agent gained most.
numbers: Base Qwen3-32B: acc 40.25, robust 11.86, trap 43.46. MDAgent: 29.70 / 10.34 / 40.34. DyLAN: 32.11 / 8.11 / 41.69. ECR-Agent: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75; ablation: add DCI 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32. Text says the agent frameworks have 'high trap rates'.
limits: The text and the table disagree on the trap rate; I trust the table. No independent run of ECR-Agent. Multi-agent systems were built on a different prompt pipeline, so a drop may be a pipeline effect.
agent_relevance: Claim K16 about debate should be softened: debate hurt accuracy here, but I cannot show it increased fixation.

source: Choi et al. (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?
finding: Across seven benchmarks, majority voting over independent samples gave most of the gain usually credited to multi-agent debate. Theory: debate is a martingale on agents' belief in the right answer, so debate alone does not raise expected accuracy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct average accuracy over 7 benchmarks: single agent 0.7205; decentralized debate T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; centralized debate T=2 0.6551; majority voting 0.7691. Arithmetics: single 0.8140, voting 0.9900, centralized debate 0.43-0.55.
limits: Benchmarks are not trap sets. Voting works when per-sample accuracy for the right answer is above chance; on a shared-prior trap the majority is the wrong answer (see d10). Table partly garbled in extraction; rows quoted are clean ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, first half: independent sampling beats debate in general. Not shown on Einstellung-type items.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Different LLMs make the same mistakes far more often than chance. Larger and more accurate models have more correlated errors, even across providers and architectures. So independent samples from different models share a prior.
numbers: Over 350 LLMs. On HELM, pairs of models agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong (uniform choice among wrong options would give about 33%). More accurate models were more correlated.
limits: Multiple-choice and a resume task, not method fixation. Read abstract, introduction and the first results; appendices not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, second half: voting over different models or personas cannot be assumed to break a shared set. Independent framing (different problem statements) is the untested remedy.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts: reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Exp 1 and 2 re-opened
finding: Elo-odds figures confirmed. Exp 1: each 100 Elo lost cut the odds of finding the shorter mate by a factor of 3.67. Exp 2 (four problems): factor 1.82 per 100 Elo. The familiar solution cut experts to the level of players about 3 SD weaker.
numbers: Exp 1: B=.013, SE=.005, Z=8.4, p=.004. Fitted probability of finding the short solution: Grand Master (Elo 2550) .64, IM (2450) .32, Master (2350) .12, Candidate Master (2150) .01. Observed on the 2-solution problem as read from the text: GM all found it, IM 50%, Master 18%, Candidate Master 0%; every expert found it when only the 1-solution version was shown. Weaker players on the 1-solution problem: Class A 63%, Class B 13%, Class C 0%. Exp 2: B=.006, SE=.0016, Z=3.72, p=.0002; fitted P(find) Elo 2500 .87, Elo 2300 .67, Elo 2100 .37. Class A vs IM/GM 91% vs 92%; Class B vs Masters 66% vs 69%; Class C vs Candidate Masters 47% vs 35%.
quote: reduced the odds of finding the shorter solution by a factor of 3.67
limits: Small cells in Exp 1. The fitted values differ from the observed ones (fitted GM .64, observed all GMs succeeded). The 3.67 and 1.82 come from different problems and are not interchangeable. The printed Table 2 is scrambled in text extraction; I used the text paragraph.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 for the chess side: the figures in K06 are right. Skill reduces the effect but at 3 SD the loss is still large; use as the reference for bigger model is less fixated, not immune.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts, verbal protocols and expert forecasts (Exp 1)
finding: All players first noticed the familiar mate, then said they were looking for something shorter. Those who failed spent as long searching as those who succeeded, then declared the familiar mate best. Experts shown both solutions greatly over-predicted how many peers would find the short one.
numbers: Median search time before finding the short solution: GM 7 s, IM 9 s, Master 10 s. Players who failed searched 9 s (IM), 8 s (Master), 8 s (Candidate Master) before settling. 12 experts (mean Elo 2231, SD 150) predicted 86% of IMs, 74% of Masters, 59% of Candidate Masters would find it; actual 50%, 18%, 0%.
limits: Verbal protocol, small groups. Time and speech are weak proxies for what the player actually considered; the gaze study (d13) is the stronger test.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, human side: 'I am searching' can be sincere and still empty. A detector must look at what new routes appear in the trace, not at the claim of searching.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect. Exp 1-3 re-opened
finding: The fixation survived failing and then being shown that a better answer exists: players who first failed the 2-solution problem were slower on the 1-solution version than players who saw only the 1-solution version. A larger skill-matched comparison in the later experiment was significant.
numbers: First experiment (Candidate Masters): 1-solution only: all found it, mean 79 s (SD 25); after the 2-solution problem they settled on smothered mate in mean 37 s (SD 20), then found the short one in mean 148 s (SD 90) when shown the 1-solution problem; t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2 (about 5 vs 5 players). Later experiment (three skill levels): players with no prior exposure solved in roughly half the time of the Einstellung group from Bilalic et al. 2008 Exp 1, t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65; skill by group interaction F(2,40)=0.9, p>.40.
limits: The first comparison is not significant and tiny. The later one compares to a historical group, not a randomised one.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 human side: removal of the familiar route does not remove its pull. Test by adding a 'route ruled out' line and measuring variants of that route in the next attempt.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022/2023) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect, re-opened: the Luchins thesis tables
finding: All Luchins counts in K01-K05 re-confirmed against the paper's text. One typo found IN THE PAPER (not only in our b05): the time-pressure paragraph prints 0.99 vs 0.55 for C3/C4, but its own counts (94/98 and 100/153) give 0.96 vs 0.65. The raw counts are right.
numbers: Plain 128/155 = .83 (C1/C2) and 100/155 = .65 (C3/C4); controls 0/155 on both. Don't-be-blind (DBB) 87/153 = .57 and 57/153 = .37. Alternating training 20/124 = .16 vs plain 97/121 = .80. Speedy 95/98 = .97 vs plain 126/153 = .82 (C1/C2) and 94/98 = .96 vs 100/153 = .65 (C3/C4). Counts are re-coded by the authors from percentages in the thesis tables.
quote: The speedy group, therefore, showed a stronger Einstellung effect than the plain group
limits: Still second-hand: this is a re-coding, not the 1942 monograph. Model beta values are tuned per condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 Luchins side: counts hold up. The single point of failure remains the thesis itself, which I could not open.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022/2023) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect, developmental section
finding: In Luchins' own data the set grew with age. The authors re-analysed 504 subjects in four age groups. Luchins himself found no strong effect of IQ or education, but later work (Luchins and Luchins 1959; Ross 1952) found the effect rose with age with IQ controlled.
numbers: N = 504 subjects, four ranks (primary school, junior high, senior high, college freshmen). Share using the long method on C1/C2 rose with age: r(503) = 0.19, p < .001; share using the direct method fell: r(503) = -0.18, p < .001. In the model a lower learning rate imitated the age pattern.
limits: Small correlations. Age is mixed with years of practice and with schooling in a fixed method. The 1959 and 1952 sources were quoted, not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the age effect is real in Luchins' data but is best read as more history with one method gives more set, not as more capable gives more rigid. Maps to in-context history length, not to model size.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharyya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set? re-read
finding: Only DeCaro-style maths equivalence items, six per cell, and the main metric is answer correctness (exact match), not strategy used. Step counts do not move. So the study cannot show a set or its absence.
numbers: Few-shot, exact match (6 items per cell): GPT-4o shortcut-only 0.33, shortcut after complex 0.66, complex only 0.66, complex then shortcut 0.83. Llama-3.1-70B: 0, 0.16, 0, 0.66. Llama-3.1-8B: 0.16, 0, 0, 0. With zero-shot chain of thought: GPT-4o 0.66, 0.66, 0.83, 0.83; steps 3 in every cell. One item is 0.17 of a cell.
limits: Order effect and difficulty are mixed; no control for the in-context examples' own content. Three models only, all pre-reasoning-model.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open; it needs 50+ items per cell, strategy as the outcome, and a reasoning-model arm. A design with problems that have a trained long method and a shorter method is easy to build for code and arithmetic.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
finding: In controlled puzzles, reasoning models find the right answer early on easy problems and keep exploring wrong ones (overthinking). At high complexity they fixate on early wrong answers and cannot recover, and effort in tokens drops near collapse.
numbers: Four puzzle families, complexity varied by size. Tower of Hanoi: simple problems (N=1-4) show early accuracy that declines over the trace; moderate (N=5-7) improve later; collapse beyond a model-specific complexity with accuracy near zero.
limits: Published critiques argue some collapses reflect output-token limits and infeasible instances; I did not open them. Fixation here is on a wrong answer, not on a trained method.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and gap 10: the trace position of the first correct answer is a measurable signal; a detector can compare the position of the first answer with the length of what follows.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Reasoning models often use a hint and do not say so. Reading the chain of thought for a statement about what drove the answer is therefore a weak detector.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1, 6 hint types. Average faithfulness 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (R1); misalignment hints 20% and 29%. Reveal rate often below 20%. Outcome RL raised faithfulness then plateaued at an average of 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA. Harder questions: 44% (Claude) and 32% (R1) relative drop in faithfulness.
limits: Hints in the prompt, not fixation on a method. Models studied are early 2025 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a trace detector must use behaviour (did new routes appear) and not the model's own statements about its search.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning (abstract only)
finding: Going from few-shot to many-shot raised performance across tasks, and many-shot learning could override pretraining biases, which few-shot could not.
numbers: Not read. Abstract states significant gains with hundreds or thousands of examples.
limits: Abstract only. Shows that dose of in-context examples changes behaviour, not that it creates a set.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 indirect: dose matters for in-context learning in general. A dose-response test for a trained method (0, 1, 5, 10, 20 examples) is still not published as far as I found.

source: Lu et al. (2022) Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them (abstract only)
finding: The order of few-shot examples can move results from near state of the art to random guess, at all model sizes. The good order does not transfer between models.
numbers: Not read. Abstract: entropy-based ordering gave a 13% relative gain.
limits: Abstract only; classification tasks.
agent_relevance: Order of examples is a real lever in LLMs, as block vs interleave is in Luchins (d14). Supports testing interleaved vs blocked examples.

source: Han et al. (2024) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (abstract only)
finding: Reasoning can be compressed with a stated token budget at a slight accuracy cost; the budget choice matters. No fixation measure.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Abstract only. Does not test rigidity.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: shows a budget can be set in the prompt, but nobody I found has measured trap-set fixation against budget.
